english: One more penalty. If Gonzalo Montiel scores, Argentina will be world champions.

In midfield, the captain stands waiting, arm around a teammate's shoulder. He is thirty-five. He has lost four finals with his country, and six years ago said he would quit the national team. The World Cup final in Qatar may be his last chance.
As Montiel runs up, the captain looks up at the sky. The sky he still points to after almost every goal, to dedicate it to his grandmother.
Twenty-five years earlier, a doctor in Rosario saw that this boy was barely growing. So every night the boy gave himself a small injection in the leg.
Almost four years after the final in Qatar, Argentina reached another World Cup final. Two days later he sat down and wrote a short message. In it were two Spanish words. Me vacié. I emptied myself.

He never talked much. He just played football. So how did a quiet boy who was too small carry a whole country? It all began on a small pitch in Rosario, on an afternoon when a kids' team was short of players.
In that message he also thanked his family. Without them there would have been no career. And the first person who believed in him was his grandmother.
It was a small neighbourhood club called Grandoli, in Rosario, Argentina. Coach Salvador Aparicio was looking for anyone who could play.
By the touchline was a woman called Celia. She had come to watch her grandson Matías play. She had also brought his younger brother, a boy of four or five.
She pointed at the little one. The coach looked at him and hesitated. The boy was tiny, much smaller than the others. But Celia would not give up. She kept begging him to let the boy on.
In the end Aparicio agreed. He put him on the wing, right next to Celia, and told her: if he cries, you take him off.
At first he barely touched the ball. But when it came to him again, he took it with his left foot and ran past one boy after another. He did not cry. Later he remembered scoring two goals that day.
In that first game the other boys were two or three years older. Some were almost twice his size. But it didn't matter.
From then on Aparicio never took him off again. And it was Celia who took him to every training session and every game.

That boy was Lionel Andrés Messi. He was born in Rosario on the twenty-fourth of June 1987, the third son of Jorge and Celia. Yes, his mother was also called Celia, just like his grandmother. His father worked at a steel factory. His mother worked in a small workshop making magnets.
He had two older brothers, Rodrigo and Matías. Later his little sister María Sol was born and the family was complete.
Rosario, a working city on the Paraná river, has factories, a port, and two football clubs that split the city in half: Newell's Old Boys and Rosario Central.
The family lived in a simple house in the south of the city, in La Bajada. The brothers played football in the street until dark. Lionel was always the smallest, and always the one with the ball.

He went to a public school a few streets from home, School Number 66. Years later the neighbourhood got a mural of his face. The words on it said he came from another galaxy, and from this neighbourhood.
At home everyone called him Leo. Later, because he was so small and so fast, his family and teammates gave him another name. La Pulga. The Flea.
His mother says at home he was quite cheeky and stubborn. He hated losing at anything, even cards. But on the pitch, thanks to that stubbornness, he never gave up on a ball.
His father and brothers were Newell's Old Boys fans, the red-and-black half of the city. On match days the whole family went to the stadium together. Leo already knew who he wanted to play for.
At six he joined the club his whole family loved, Newell's Old Boys. In one of his first games the team won six–nil, he scored four.
The players born in 1987 became a team people in Rosario still talk about. They called it "La Máquina del '87", the Machine of 87. For years it almost never lost.
Sometimes opponents asked for a deal before kickoff: if it got to six–nil, the game would stop. Even at six–nil, Lionel was still annoyed if he himself hadn't scored.

Coach Carlos Marconi has told this story many times. He promised Leo an alfajor, a sweet chocolate-covered biscuit, for every goal. Leo scored so many that he had to change it: two, but only for headers. Soon after, the smallest boy on the pitch scored a header. He turned to him, smiled and held up two fingers.
Teammates from then remember small things. Before every game he cleaned his boots carefully and taped his own ankles like a pro. He was only eight or nine.
One teammate remembers a derby against Rosario Central. Leo beat one defender again and again, until the defender's father shouted from the stands telling his son to kick Leo.
The league recorded his goals. More than two hundred in five years. People in Rosario say the real number is much higher.
His size was always a problem. Big defenders kicked his legs, and some parents on the touchline shouted to stop him any way possible. Every time he got up and asked for the ball again.
Coaches wanted to protect him. They told him to pass earlier so he wouldn't get hurt. He kept dribbling. If he lost the ball he rushed back to win it.
But in 1998, when he was ten, grandmother Celia died. The person who had brought him to football was gone.
Years later he said she was a very big love, and he still finds it hard to talk about her. He dedicates goals to her. After many goals he looks up and points to the sky.
His mother says that after his grandmother died, the boy often talked to her and asked her to help him. He rarely told anyone. He wasn't a child who showed his feelings.
Without her he kept playing. He was still the best player on the team. But something was wrong, and everyone could see it. The other kids grew, and he didn't.
Newell's took him to endocrinologist Diego Schwarzstein. The club wanted to know why its top young talent was so much smaller than the others.
Tests showed Lionel's body didn't produce enough growth hormone. Without treatment he would be ten to fifteen centimetres shorter than normal.
One word would follow him for many years. Small. The best player of his age in Rosario, and also the smallest.
There was a treatment: every night a small injection in the leg, not one night missed. But the medicine was very expensive, more than nine hundred dollars a month.
From a young age he learned to inject himself. Every night: a needle into his own leg. A teammate remembers seeing him inject before a game as if it were nothing.
A friend's father once taught him to drive on an empty country road. Lionel was only eleven.

Every month his father sat and did the maths. The medicine ate a lot of his factory wages. Help from insurance and the club didn't last. Without treatment, his son's football would end before it began.
So they looked for a club willing to pay. At that time Lionel went to Buenos Aires for a trial at River Plate, one of the biggest clubs in the country.
In 2026 Messi himself told this story. He trained there about ten days and River wanted to keep him. They even offered to pay for treatment. But first Newell's had to agree to let him go.
That was the closest he came to a big club at home.
But when he went back to Newell's to ask to leave, they refused, and River's offer vanished. He says that was the end of it. Then help came from across the ocean.

An Argentine agent in Barcelona received a video of a boy from Rosario. He and a colleague showed it to the club, and Barcelona invited him for a trial. In September 2000 father and son flew to Spain. He was thirteen.
At Newell's his teammates didn't know where he had gone. They were told he was ill.
In Barcelona he played with older boys. Sporting director Carles Rexach came to watch.
According to one account, from his seat to the pitch Rexach only needed three or four minutes. It took him fifteen, because he couldn't take his eyes off the boy.
At the trial was Cesc Fàbregas, who later played with Messi for many years. Before the game the coach told Cesc to mark the new boy from Argentina tightly.
Cesc looked at him and thought this would be easy. The boy was tiny. A few seconds later Fàbregas was on the ground and the Argentine boy had gone with the ball.

Later Rexach said he told the club: sign him now, don't think about it. But the bosses hesitated. He was a foreigner, very small, and needed expensive treatment. Weeks passed and nobody decided anything.
For Jorge the waiting was miserable. He had given up a steady job at the factory. Father and son lived in a hotel in a foreign land, not knowing whether they would ever have a home there.
After more than two months of waiting, Jorge called Rexach and said very clearly: if it wasn't sorted soon, they would go home.
On the fourteenth of December 2000, Rexach met two agents at a tennis club in Barcelona. With no paper at hand, he wrote the promise on a paper napkin. Barcelona would sign Lionel Messi.
One of Barcelona's leaders, Joan Gaspart, later admitted the napkin had no legal value. It was only to reassure a father about to leave. And it worked.
Rexach signed, and the two agents signed as witnesses. Years later the napkin was auctioned in London for more than seven hundred and sixty thousand pounds.
Barcelona agreed to pay for the treatment and find his father a job. In February 2001 the whole family moved to Spain.
At thirteen Leo didn't fully understand everything. He only knew he would play football, and would keep having injections, now paid by Barcelona.
For the boy from La Bajada, it was a dream. For his family, it was the start of the hardest year of their lives.
Things weren't as they had imagined. Because of foreign-player rules, Lionel couldn't play officially for many months. And in only his second youth game he broke his leg.
His mother, two brothers and sister were homesick. They couldn't get used to the new city, and before the first year was over they decided to go back to Rosario.
Jorge asked his son if he wanted to go back with the family. Lionel said no. Years later he summed it up in one sentence: I wanted to continue, and my father stayed with me.
So the family was split between two continents. Lionel and his father stayed in Barcelona. Part of Jorge's salary paid for life there. The rest was sent to Rosario, for his wife and children.
Now a boy of only thirteen lived eleven thousand kilometres from his mother, two brothers and sister.
On Sundays there was nobody around him. He played video games with his father in the small flat. Then, according to biographer Guillem Balagué, he went to his room and cried into his pillow.
My father was always by my side, Messi said later, and the two of us went through so many sad things together.
At the club he barely spoke. At the first training, the coach asked what position he played; he mumbled one word, "forward", and sat in the corner of the dressing room.
Teammates didn't know what to think. Fàbregas says for a long time they thought he couldn't speak. He could. He was just very shy. He didn't talk much. He just played football.
They called him "el enano", the dwarf. But when the ball reached his feet, nobody laughed any more.

Little by little he found his place. His team was full of boys born in 1987 like him: Cesc Fàbregas, Gerard Piqué and many others. They played with three defenders, attacked all the time, and people started calling them the Baby Dream Team.
Bit by bit the quiet boy began joking with teammates. They found him funny, crazy about cards and video games. He hated losing those games just as much as losing on the pitch.
One season they lost almost no games, and Messi scored more than thirty goals. Piqué, much taller, always protected him on the pitch.

Coach Tito Vilanova later became one of the most important people in Messi's life. The story goes that in one game the team led three–nil after three minutes. Tito turned to his assistant and joked: what do we tell the kids at half-time, when it's eight–nil?
Every night he injected. And every year he grew a little taller. By his teens the treatment had worked.
Later he was about one metre seventy. Still one of the smallest players on the pitch. But that was enough.
Years later his doctor in Rosario, Diego Schwarzstein, said plainly: he only helped a boy grow. Everything else Messi did himself.
In November 2003 Barcelona played a friendly in Porto, opening a new stadium. Coach Frank Rijkaard sent on sixteen-year-old youth player Lionel Messi. On the other bench was José Mourinho.
That night was just a friendly. But the boy had played for the first team. That season he climbed through four different Barcelona teams.
His official debut was the sixteenth of October 2004, against Espanyol. He came on at the end, wearing number thirty. He was seventeen.
At the time he was the youngest Barcelona player ever to play in La Liga. Later a younger player broke that record. He stayed at Barcelona seventeen years.
At the club everyone remembers that off the pitch he was shy, almost silent. An agent remembers his legs were the thinnest he had ever seen.
But in the dressing room someone had seen that talent. Ronaldinho, the best player in the world, protected the quiet boy.

Other Brazilian players like Deco, Sylvinho, Thiago Motta also looked after the boy. Ronaldinho sat next to him in the dressing room, invited him to the Brazilians' table. Leo says he learned a lot from them, especially from him.
Not everyone was kind. French teammate Ludovic Giuly remembers some older players kicking his legs in training to see how he'd react. He never complained. He just got up and played on.
On the first of May 2005, against Albacete, Messi came on in the final minutes. Ronaldinho lobbed the ball over the defence, and Messi chipped it over the goalkeeper. But the referee gave offside.
A few minutes later Ronaldinho did exactly the same again. And Messi did exactly the same again. This time the goal counted.
Ronaldinho bent down and the boy jumped on his back. It was his first official goal for Barcelona. Ronaldinho says he was proud to witness that beginning.

Let me stop a moment to tell you about myself. I'm Kamil, twenty-one. I've been doing YouTube since 2014, when I was nine. Most of the channels went nowhere. A hundred thousand subscribers and the silver button are my childhood dream. If this story means something to you, please subscribe so I can take one more step. Now, let's go back.

In spring 2006 Barcelona reached the Champions League knockout stage, and Messi tormented Chelsea at Stamford Bridge. Two weeks later, in the second leg, he tore a thigh muscle and left the pitch crying.
The whole Camp Nou stood and applauded. Rijkaard put his arm around him. Messi was eighteen.
Barcelona then won the final in Paris. Messi didn't play. He was so sad he didn't join the celebrations. Years later he said he deeply regrets that night.
From 2004 another question had appeared. Messi had lived in Spain since thirteen, and the Spanish federation wanted him to play for them.
Argentina's youth coaches heard about it and acted. In June 2004 they organised a U20 friendly against Paraguay, mainly so Messi could play and be tied to the country.
Argentina won eight–nil. Messi says he really could have played for Spain. But in his heart he was from Rosario.

Cesc Fàbregas, his old academy friend, said it would have been great if Leo had played for Spain. A few years later Spain won the World Cup without him. Argentina's national team waited eleven more years for a trophy.
In 2005, at the U20 World Cup in the Netherlands, he was the best player of the tournament. He scored six goals, including two penalties in the final against Nigeria. Argentina were world champions.
He also won the tournament's Golden Ball and Golden Boot, for best player and top scorer. For the first time the boy from Rosario was a champion in the sky-blue-and-white shirt.
Six weeks later, in August 2005, he debuted for the national team in a friendly against Hungary in Budapest. He was sent on in the second half.

At his very first touch a defender pulled his shirt. Messi yanked his arm free, and the arm hit the defender. The referee showed a red card. He had been on the pitch less than a minute. According to the press, he cried leaving the pitch.
Years later he said he thought then: I've just come on and been sent off, they'll never call me up again.
A teammate on the pitch that night ran over to argue with the referee for him. It was Lionel Scaloni. Remember this name, because years later he will come back into the story.
But they did call him again. In March 2006, against Croatia, he scored his first goal for Argentina. That summer he went to his first World Cup, in Germany.
Against Serbia and Montenegro he came on as a sub, scored the sixth goal, a six–nil win. At eighteen he was the youngest Argentine to score at a World Cup.
In that game he also set up Hernán Crespo. He played as if he belonged there.
In the quarter-final against hosts Germany, Argentina were leading. Then the coach used the last substitution on someone else, and the game slipped away. Argentina lost on penalties.
Messi sat on the bench the whole match. For the first time a World Cup ended while he only sat and watched. He said nothing to the press. Once again he didn't talk much.
In April 2007, in the Copa del Rey semi-final against Getafe, Messi got the ball in his own half. He beat one man, then a second, then a third, then the goalkeeper, and scored.
He started on the right wing, near the halfway line. In about ten seconds he went almost the whole pitch, the ball as if glued to his left foot.
All of Argentina recognised that goal. It was almost exactly the goal Diego Maradona, Argentina's greatest hero, scored against England at the 1986 World Cup. Messi was nineteen.
Barcelona won that game five–two. But in the second leg Getafe won four–nil, and Barcelona were out. Even a goal like that couldn't save the team.
Those were hard years for Barcelona. Ronaldinho declined, the team kept losing, the club needed a fresh start. Messi improved month by month, but was often injured.
In the message written after the 2026 final there is another line: I swear I always gave everything. And it's true. But for many years with Argentina, giving everything still wasn't enough to win.
In summer 2007, at the Copa América in Venezuela, Argentina reached the final against Brazil. Messi had just turned twenty. Brazil won three–nil.
He played the full ninety minutes and could do almost nothing. In the end he had to watch Brazil celebrate.
It was his first final with the national team. Nobody knew he would lose three more before winning one.
In 2008 he wanted to go to the Olympics in Beijing. Barcelona didn't want to release him, as the Olympics weren't on the official calendar. The case went all the way to a special sports court.
Messi said it was his decision, and he would never have another chance at the Olympics. The court ruled for the clubs.
But Barcelona had a new coach, Pep Guardiola. He had won Olympic gold in Barcelona in 1992, and he understood. He let Messi go.
At those Olympics he scored two goals, against Ivory Coast and the Netherlands.

In the final against Nigeria, in front of about ninety thousand spectators, he slipped a through ball to close friend Ángel Di María, and Di María lobbed the goalkeeper. It was the only goal. Argentina won Olympic gold.
He says some things in football only come once. It was his only Olympics. He considers that medal one of his most precious wins. Meanwhile at Barcelona, Guardiola was about to give him a new role.
Guardiola started with a surprise. He told Ronaldinho, Messi's idol, that he was no longer in the plans. Barcelona would be built around the twenty-one-year-old.
That summer Ronaldinho moved to Milan. Before leaving he told Leo to take the number ten shirt. The quiet boy who once jumped on his back now wore his number, and was the team's star.
In May 2009 Barcelona went to the Bernabéu to play Real Madrid. According to journalist Martí Perarnau's book, the night before, Guardiola called Messi into his room and showed him a video.
Between Real's midfield and defence there was a gap. Guardiola told him to play on the right, then drift inside, into that gap. With the ball, run straight at goal.
According to that book, Guardiola kept the plan secret until the last moment.
Messi didn't play on the wing, or as a striker. He played between the two, so defenders didn't know who should follow him. Barcelona won six–two in Madrid. Messi scored two.
A few days later, in the semi-final at Stamford Bridge, Barcelona were losing in the ninety-third minute. Messi passed to Andrés Iniesta, and Iniesta scored. Barcelona were in the final.
Three weeks later, in Rome, they faced Manchester United in the Champions League final. Before the game Guardiola showed the team a video of the season, with music from the film Gladiator.
Before that final Leo remembered Paris, the night he felt left out and stood outside the celebrations. This time, he said, he needed to enjoy it more.
In the seventieth minute Xavi crossed into the box. And the smallest player on the pitch jumped higher than the defender and headed over the tall goalkeeper Edwin van der Sar.
Van der Sar was nearly two metres tall. Messi was about one metre seventy. The boy who was once too small beat that goalkeeper in the air.
Barcelona won two–nil.
That year they won every possible trophy. La Liga, the Copa del Rey, the Champions League, and three more. Six out of six, something no team had ever done.
The sixth trophy came in December in Abu Dhabi, against Argentine side Estudiantes. In extra time Messi scored the winning goal with his chest.
A few weeks earlier he had won his first Ballon d'Or (Golden Ball), the award for the best player in the world. He was twenty-two. The boy who was once too small was now the best.
In January 2011, at the Ballon d'Or ceremony in Zurich, the three finalists all came from one place: La Masia, Barcelona's youth academy. They were Xavi, Andrés Iniesta and Lionel Messi.
Most guessed Xavi or Iniesta. They had just won the World Cup with Spain, Iniesta scoring the winner in the final. But the winner was Messi, for the second year in a row.
He said he didn't expect it. He said Xavi and Iniesta deserved it as much as he did, even more. They were the first to congratulate him.
All three held a press conference together, and all three said the same thing. This award belongs to the whole team.
Years later Xavi remembered meeting him on a trip: a polite, humble boy, not at all arrogant. Xavi never imagined he would become the best player in history.

In May 2011, at Wembley, Barcelona again beat Manchester United in the Champions League final, Messi scoring with a powerful low shot from outside the box. But the most emotional moment came at the end. That spring doctors had removed a tumour from defender Éric Abidal's liver. Carles Puyol gave the captain's armband to Abidal, so he could lift the cup himself.

In May 2012 Guardiola had his last home game as Barcelona coach. Messi scored all four goals. After the fourth he ran to the touchline to hug his coach. Guardiola joked that Leo had taken all the glory all season, and he couldn't even be jealous.
In December 2012 he broke a forty-year-old record. Gerd Müller had scored eighty-five goals in a year. Messi ended that year with ninety-one, five of them in a single Champions League game.

Müller wasn't upset. He called Leo a giant, joking that his only fault was not playing for Bayern. A few weeks later Leo sent him a Barcelona shirt with a handwritten note: with respect and admiration, a hug. Leo himself said trophies matter more than records.
Life off the pitch changed too. His girlfriend was Antonela Roccuzzo, a Rosario girl he had known since childhood. In November 2012 their first son was born, named Thiago.
Two months after Thiago was born, Leo said becoming a father changes you completely. He said now his son comes first.

In January 2013 he won his fourth Ballon d'Or in a row. Nobody had won it four times. But that winter Tito Vilanova was being treated for cancer. He had been his coach since La Masia, now in charge of the first team. And Abidal had just returned after a liver transplant. In his speech in Zurich Leo forgot to thank the two of them. Afterwards he apologised. He once said Tito believed in him since Leo was just a boy who often sat on the bench.
At Barcelona he was like a god. With the national team it was different.
Argentina hadn't won a major trophy since 1993, when Messi was six. Now a whole country wanted him to end the wait.

At the 2010 World Cup in South Africa, Argentina's coach was Diego Maradona himself. In the quarter-final in Cape Town they met Germany. Germany scored in the third minute and won four–nil. Messi didn't score a single goal all tournament.
After the game Maradona said he had seen Messi crying in the dressing room.
He said: anyone who says he doesn't love this shirt is really stupid.
Because that was exactly what many Argentines said. He went to Spain at thirteen, never played for an Argentine club, and didn't sing the anthem before games.
They called players like him "pecho frío". Cold chest (rib cage). Someone without enough fire when it matters. For many, his silence meant he didn't care.
At the 2011 Copa América, on home soil, he was booed by the crowd. His father said his son was very hurt and didn't understand why they whistled at him.

That Copa's coach, Sergio Batista, wanted to use him like Barcelona did. It didn't work. Messi said comparing Argentina with Barcelona was a mistake. Barcelona was a team that had played together for years.
Argentina were knocked out in the quarter-final, on penalties, by Uruguay. At home the criticism didn't stop. So he did what he always did. He didn't talk much. He just played football.
In April 2014 Tito Vilanova died aged forty-five. According to Tito's former assistant, six days earlier Leo visited him at home and talked for hours. The coach of his first big team was gone.

Less than two months later, at the World Cup in Brazil, Messi carried the whole team. After his first goal, against Bosnia, he looked up at the sky as he often did. He scored four in the group stage. Against Iran he scored the winner in the ninety-first minute.
He was man of the match four times. Argentina reached a World Cup final for the first time in twenty-four years.
In the semi-final they beat the Netherlands on penalties. Defender Javier Mascherano said without Leo Argentina couldn't have gone so far.
The final was at the Maracanã, Rio de Janeiro, against Germany again. Messi had chances, so did his teammates. No one scored. Then in extra time Mario Götze did.
After the game Messi received the tournament's Golden Ball, for the best player. On his way up he walked past the World Cup trophy without looking.
He said he didn't care about the tournament's Golden Ball. Then FIFA president Sepp Blatter later said Messi kept muttering one sentence: the best, but not the champion.
It was his second lost final. Three years later he said that defeat would follow him forever.
In 2015, at the Copa América in Chile, Argentina reached the final again. Against Chile, nil–nil after one hundred and twenty minutes. Messi scored his penalty. Two teammates missed, and Chile won.
Just a month earlier he had won the Champions League again with Barcelona in Berlin, alongside Neymar and Luis Suárez. With his club he won everything. With his country he kept losing.
Chile's coach that night was an Argentine, Jorge Sampaoli. Two years later he coached Argentina.
After the game Messi wrote that in football nothing hurts more than losing a final. He had lost three.
In June 2016 there was one more chance. A special Copa América in the USA, exactly a hundred years after the first tournament. The final was at MetLife Stadium, near New York.
And the opponent was Chile again. Again nobody scored. Again it went to penalties.
Messi took Argentina's first penalty. He leaned back and the ball flew over the bar.
Chile won the shootout. It was his fourth lost final with Argentina. Three in a row, in three years.
Lucas Biglia's penalty was also saved. But the miss everyone remembers is the captain's.
A few minutes later, in the tunnel, a reporter stopped him. The quiet man said only a few words: it's over, I'm leaving the national team.
The whole team was crushed. Sergio Agüero was his best friend in the squad, sharing a room with him at almost every camp for years. Agüero said that defeat broke Leo.
Messi cried on his shoulder for about twenty-five seconds, like a little boy, repeating: it's not for me, it's not for me.
That night, according to the team's fitness coach, at two in the morning Leo was still awake and sobbing.

Then something he didn't expect happened. In Argentina people began begging him to stay. The president called him and said publicly Messi was the best thing Argentina had. On a rainy Saturday in Buenos Aires hundreds gathered at the Obelisk with banners. "Don't go, Leo."
Somewhere in Argentina, fifteen-year-old Enzo Fernández also wrote a letter asking him not to go. Six years later he would play beside him in a World Cup final.
The country that called him cold now wanted him back. Less than two months later he announced his return. In his first game back he scored.
Asked why he came back, he said he loved his country and this shirt too much, and wanted to help.
Later he explained why he had wanted to leave. Not only because of losing, he said, but also because things outside football hurt him and his family.
He also said he wasn't sure whether he had told his father before speaking in the tunnel. He just felt, at that moment, it had to be like that.
That summer a Spanish court convicted Messi and his father of tax fraud on image-rights money. The prison sentences were converted into fines, as usual in that country for first-time offenders.
Messi testified in court that his father handled the money. By then the family had paid back about five million euros.

In June 2017 Leo married Antonela in Rosario, the city where they grew up. He could have married anywhere, but chose his hometown. About two hundred and fifty guests came, including teammates from Barcelona and Argentina. Thiago and his little brother Mateo sat in the front row, and Leo's brothers and sister signed as witnesses.

On the pitch Argentina struggled. Before the last World Cup 2018 qualifier they weren't even in the qualifying places. They had to win in Quito, high in the Andes, where they hadn't won for sixteen years.

That night in Argentina the streets were almost empty. People watched in bars and at home. In La Plata the band U2 even delayed its concert so fans could watch the game on a big screen. Then in the very first minute Ecuador scored, and the bars went silent.
Then Messi scored three goals. Argentina won three–one and got the ticket to Russia. Even Ecuador fans applauded him.
In the dressing room the team sang a song aimed at the critics. Mascherano said missing the World Cup would have been the end for many of the lads.
After the game Messi said Argentina missing the World Cup would have been crazy. Now, he said, they were at peace.
Coach Jorge Sampaoli had a line many remember: Messi doesn't owe Argentina a World Cup. Football owes Messi a World Cup.
Russia didn't pay that debt. In the first game, against Iceland, Messi missed a penalty.
The goalkeeper who saved it, Hannes Halldórsson, is also a (film) director in Iceland. He said he had studied how Messi takes penalties before the game.
Then Argentina lost three–nil to Croatia. They beat Nigeria, with a goal by Messi, which he called a great relief.
In the round of sixteen, against France in Kazan, Antonela came with Thiago and Mateo, the two kids in shirts printed Papá. Argentina lost four–three. Once again Messi went home empty-handed.

In the 2026 farewell message he also wrote that leaving the national team was a decision that hurt him, and still hurts, deep in his heart. He had felt that pain once before, in Barcelona. There, the end started with a few nights in Europe that nobody at the club wants to remember.

Everything had begun to crack. In 2018 they beat Roma easily in the first leg, then lost three–nil in Rome. A year later it happened again: they beat Liverpool three–nil at home, then lost four–nil in Liverpool.
A few days after Anfield he said the coach wasn't to blame. The fault was mainly his and his teammates'.
In 2019 he got his sixth Ballon d'Or, the most in history. But it couldn't mend the breakdown around him.
And in August 2020, in Lisbon, Bayern Munich beat Barcelona eight–two.
Ten days after Lisbon, Messi sent the club an official letter. He wanted to leave. Barcelona refused, saying the contract didn't allow it.
His father flew to Barcelona to meet the club. In the end Messi said he would stay one more year, because he would never take the club he loved to court.

About six weeks after Lisbon, Barcelona pushed out Luis Suárez, his close friend. Leo wrote that Suárez deserved a proper farewell, not to be thrown out like that. But nothing surprised him any more, he wrote.
Then in November 2020 Diego Maradona died. Argentina mourned for days. The man who defended Messi after Cape Town was gone, and the country still had no major trophy with Messi.
That year the whole world was in lockdown because of the pandemic. In summer 2021 the Copa América was moved to Brazil at the last minute. The final was at the Maracanã, against Brazil.
Because of the pandemic the stadium had almost no fans. One of the biggest games of his life with Argentina would be played almost in silence.
The players had been away from their families for weeks. Before the final, in the dressing room, the quiet captain stood up. Someone filmed it.
For years people said he was too quiet to be a leader. That night he spoke.

Forty-five days without seeing our families, lads, he said. He mentioned goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez, who had just become a father and hadn't yet held his daughter. Then he finished: go out confident and calm, because we're taking this cup home.
Martínez later said he wanted to cry. Another player burst into tears just a moment later, and said he doesn't remember the rest.
In the twenty-second minute Rodrigo De Paul played a long ball to Ángel Di María, the friend Messi once set up for Olympic gold. Di María lobbed the goalkeeper. One–nil.
For the seventy minutes after that, Brazil attacked, Argentina held on. Messi had a chance for a second but missed. It didn't matter.
At the final whistle Messi knelt, covering his face with both hands. Teammates rushed in and piled on top of him until he disappeared underneath.
Then he phoned his wife and sons in Rosario. After four lost finals he finally had a trophy with the national team. He was thirty-four.

After the game Di María said the curse had to break eventually, and finally it did. Messi dedicated the trophy to his family, to the people of Argentina, and to Maradona, who he said was surely cheering for them, wherever he was.
A month later he was supposed to sign a new contract with Barcelona. But the club announced it couldn't keep him, because of debts and La Liga rules.
On the eighth of August 2021 he walked into a room at Camp Nou to say goodbye. Before saying a word he was crying.
He said he wasn't ready for this. He and his family had wanted to stay. He came to this city at thirteen and was leaving at thirty-four, with three sons, Thiago, Mateo and Ciro, all born here.
He was also sad he couldn't say goodbye to fans in the stadium. Because of the pandemic he hadn't seen them for a year and a half.
He signed for Paris Saint-Germain, but never really fitted. When the team lost, fans booed him.
Once, after a defeat, he flew to Saudi Arabia for promotion without asking the club. Paris suspended him, he apologised by video. By then everyone knew he wouldn't stay.

In November 2022 Argentina arrived at the World Cup in Qatar unbeaten in thirty-six games. The coach was Lionel Scaloni, the teammate who once defended him in Budapest. Messi was thirty-five. Everyone knew this was maybe the last chance.
In the first game, against Saudi Arabia, he scored a penalty. Then in five minutes the opponents scored twice. Argentina lost two–one. One of the biggest shocks in World Cup history.
After the game Messi faced the press. There are no excuses, he said. The dressing room was stunned. But he asked Argentines to believe in the team: we will be more united than ever.
In the following days teammates said he talked more than ever before. The quiet captain had spoken up.
One song followed them everywhere, the fans' song Muchachos. The team sang it on the bus, in the dressing room. Messi sang along.
From then on every game was a final. Against Mexico Messi opened the scoring and Argentina won two–nil. They beat Poland, then Australia.
Against Australia he played the thousandth game of his career, and scored.
In the quarter-final against the Netherlands, Argentina led two–nil, then were pegged back to two–two in the final seconds. It went to penalties, and Argentina won.

After that game the world saw a Messi never seen before. As he was talking to TV, a Dutch player walked past. Messi turned and said, the way Rosario street people talk: "What are you looking at, fool?"
The man once called cold was now on fire. In the semi-final Argentina beat Croatia three–nil. Messi scored a penalty, then beat one of the world's top young defenders and set up Julián Álvarez.
On the eighteenth of December 2022 Argentina met France in the final. Messi scored a penalty. Di María scored next.
Two–nil. Ten minutes left. Four lost finals behind him, the trophy right in front.
Then in less than two minutes Kylian Mbappé scored twice. Two–two.
Extra time. Messi scored again. Three–two. Then Mbappé scored once more, this time from the penalty spot. Three–three.
In the last minute France had one more chance, but Emiliano Martínez saved with his leg. So after one hundred and twenty minutes the World Cup was decided on penalties.
Messi scored. Martínez saved one, France missed one. Then it was Gonzalo Montiel's turn, with the kick that could decide everything.
This is the moment at the start of the film. Montiel steps up to the ball. Messi looks up to the sky, and later said he asked God to let the game end.
Montiel scores. Lionel Messi drops to his knees on the grass.
He had lost four finals with Argentina. Had said it was over. Then came back. And now, at thirty-five, he is world champion.
Before lifting the trophy, the Emir of Qatar draped him in a traditional black robe. Then he raised the trophy high, kissed it, wouldn't let go.
Then his family came onto the pitch. His mother hugged him tight. His three sons ran to him, and he took a photo of Antonela hugging the trophy.

His two goals in the final were his sixth and seventh of the tournament. After the game he again received the tournament's Golden Ball. Eight years earlier he hadn't cared about it, because Argentina lost. This time he had the trophy as well.
At that World Cup he was the first to score in the group stage, round of sixteen, quarter-final, semi-final and final.
Later he said on TV that the trophy seemed to call him: now you can touch me.
He said he hadn't watched the final again, only highlights. At home his children copy goalkeeper Martínez's celebration.
Back in Buenos Aires, millions poured into the streets. So many that the team bus got stuck, and the players had to go by helicopter.

In March 2023, before leaving Europe, he had one more happy night in Buenos Aires. In the first home game of world champions Argentina, against Panama at the Monumental, he scored his eight-hundredth career goal. He said he always dreamed of this: celebrating with his people, at home.

That summer, his Paris contract over, he made a choice that surprised everyone. Not Barcelona. Not the huge offer from Saudi Arabia. But Inter Miami, a young club in the USA. Many thought he went there to slow down.
He explained it simply. He wanted to step away from the spotlight a bit and think more about his family. He said if it were about money, he'd have gone to Saudi Arabia.
His first game for Miami was in July 2023. He came on in the second half. In the ninety-fourth minute, at one–one, he curled a free kick into the top corner.

That first night, from the bench, he smiled at Antonela and their three sons in the stands. LeBron James and Serena Williams came too. When the ball went in, the club's co-owner David Beckham burst into tears.
A few weeks later Miami won the first trophy in its history. Slowing down? Hardly. And in October he won his eighth Ballon d'Or.
In Miami he also became a football dad. His three sons joined the club's academy, and he and Antonela often cheer on the touchline like any parents.
In 2024 Argentina reached the Copa América final again, against Colombia, in Miami. In the second half he twisted his ankle and had to leave the pitch.

On the bench he burst into tears. Teammate Leandro Paredes sat beside him. Paredes said he didn't dare look at Leo, only heard him crying. Argentina won in extra time after he had gone off. It was also friend Di María's last game.

In September 2025 he played a World Cup qualifier that he said was probably his last at home, against Venezuela in Buenos Aires. During the warm-up he fought back tears as over eighty thousand people chanted his name. He scored two. He said ending like that, at home, was what he had always dreamed of.
In December 2025 Miami won the MLS Cup for the first time. On the pitch his son Mateo juggled the ball, then pointed at his dad.
In March 2026 he scored the nine-hundredth goal of his career. He was thirty-eight, some said he was too old.
It was a game Miami didn't win, and they were knocked out of a continental cup. For him, the result mattered more than the record. And ahead there was still one more World Cup.
His father, Jorge, had always wanted to see him at one more World Cup. But just before the tournament Jorge fell seriously ill. For the first time he couldn't be there to watch his son play.
In the first game, against Algeria, he scored three. Then two against Austria, one against Jordan. Argentina easily topped the group.
And after every game, the same things. Take off boots. Grab the phone. Any message from home? That was how he knew how his father was.
He kept it hidden then, but he played while his father was ill, thousands of kilometres away. Later he admitted he never felt okay the whole tournament.
In the knockouts every game was tough. Against Cape Verde, extra time.
Against Egypt Messi missed a penalty. He didn't hang his head. He set up Cristian Romero, equalised himself, then Enzo Fernández headed the winner. Against Switzerland, extra time again.
Take off boots. Grab the phone. Message from home?

Semi-final in Atlanta, against England. England scored first. Argentina came back in the last five minutes, and in the final minute Messi crossed for the winner. Two–one. They were in the final again.
After the game Messi was choked with emotion. Then he went around the pitch hugging every teammate and staff member. Even coach Scaloni was speechless.
He had scored eight goals at that World Cup. In history, nobody had scored more goals, or played more games than him at the World Cup.
The final was on the nineteenth of July 2026, at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. The very place where ten years earlier he had said it was all over.
Before the game, in the dressing room, he told teammates to stay calm, forget everything and just think about playing.
Spain had nineteen-year-old Lamine Yamal and a team full of young players. They had the ball almost the whole game, and almost all the chances.
Still nil–nil. In a video released later, Messi is heard telling the team: guts, lads, guts.
At the end of normal time Enzo Fernández, the boy who once wrote him a letter, was sent off. Ten men, and thirty more minutes to hold on.
In the one hundred and sixth minute Ferran Torres scored. Argentina couldn't respond.
All game Messi had only one shot. The fifth time he lost a final with Argentina.

After the final whistle Messi sat on the grass. Yamal came to hug him. Messi told him to go his own way, because the future belongs to his generation. Yamal later said those words were as precious to him as a gold medal.
Scaloni broke down crying at the press conference and had to leave the room. Before the final he had said Messi was the best player ever to step on a football pitch.
The next day Messi wrote to the fans. The pain is so great, he wrote, and this wound needs time to heal.
In August 2026, less than three weeks after the final, Jorge Messi died in Rosario after a long illness, at the (venerable) age of sixty-eight.
A few days later Lionel wrote his father a letter and shared it with the whole world. It began very simply: I love you, Dad.

He wrote that he had promised his father to reach the final, so he could come and watch. But his father couldn't come. Lionel wanted to win and bring the trophy home for him. But he couldn't, he wrote. His legs had run out of strength.
He wrote that throughout the World Cup, after every game, he waited for his father's message. When none came, he understood how ill his father was.
You were my dad, my friend, my agent, he wrote. The man who quit his job in Rosario and waited in Barcelona for a paper napkin.
Since then, every time he looks up at the sky, there are two people up there.
On the thirty-first of August Messi posted the message from the start of the film. He had written it on the twenty-first of July, two days after the final, and kept it secret for six weeks.
In it he said goodbye to the national team. Me vacié, he wrote. I emptied myself. I have nothing left to give, and talented young players deserve a place. From now on I'm just one of you.
Then he added a last line: today, after what happened to my father, I am even more sure of this decision.
He didn't write about trophies or finals. He wrote about family, the fans, and his father.

On the sixth of October 2026 he played his last game for Argentina, a friendly against Benin, at the Monumental in Buenos Aires. It is River Plate's ground. The club that once wanted the tiny boy from Rosario, but didn't get him.
About eighty-five thousand people came. He walked out holding hands with his three sons. His mother watched from the stands.
A Falklands War veteran sang the anthem. Messi struggled to hold back tears. In the tenth minute the game stopped, the whole stadium applauded for a long time, and the Benin players came over to him.
He set up two goals, then scored a penalty: his hundred-and-twenty-sixth goal for Argentina, in his two-hundred-and-eighth game.
The second assist was for Nico Paz, twenty-two, a young player he said deserved a place.
After the game hundreds of drones lit up the sky above the stadium. And the boy who once sat silent in the corner of the dressing room took the microphone, in front of eighty-five thousand people.
The first thing he said was that he was thinking of his father. Then he said this was the saddest day of his career.
For weeks people argued about the refereeing at that World Cup. Messi stayed out of it. That night he said there was nothing strange. His team simply gave everything.
He said wearing Argentina's shirt is the most beautiful thing that can happen to anyone. He wants to be here all his life. Then he told fans he loves them and will miss them.
Then he walked around the pitch with his wife and three sons, as eighty-five thousand people sang: Messi isn't leaving.
He called it the saddest day of his career. Yet in the message he had written: I leave at peace, and proud.
He was too small. Too expensive. A foreigner in Spain, a stranger in Argentina. Later, people said he was too old.
But two people didn't think so. The grandmother asked the coach to let her grandson play. And the father provided enough money, crossed the ocean with his son, stayed.
He never played just for himself. He played for them. When he looks up at the sky after every goal, he is looking for them.
The cold chest Argentina used to talk about was never cold. He only hid his feelings. He kept them inside, only to burst out when he lost, or when he finally won.
And the last final, July 2026, hurt more than any. Not because of one more trophy. It was the last thing he wanted to bring home for his father.
Today he still plays in Miami. He has scored more than nine hundred goals. He no longer wears the Argentina shirt. Now, as he wrote, he is just a fan.
Maybe you're quiet. The one in the corner of the dressing room. The one thought not to care.
Leo was that boy too. He was never loud. He didn't talk much. He just played football, for the people who believed in him. At the most important moment, he spoke up. One day the whole world listened.
If you're quiet, you don't need to be loud. Keep playing. Your time to speak will come.
On the night he said goodbye to Argentina, the boy who used to say almost nothing smiled at eighty-five thousand people. I've talked more than ever, he said, and I don't want to go.
That summer Spain didn't only close Leo's last World Cup. Two weeks earlier, in Texas, they crushed the dream of another boy who wanted that trophy just as much.
The boy from a small island in the middle of the Atlantic, once called a crybaby by his teammates. His name is Cristiano Ronaldo, and his full story is right here.
